Contemptuous is an adjective that describes a person, look, tone, action, or attitude that shows deep disrespect and a strong sense that someone or something is worthless, inferior, or beneath notice.

When you are contemptuous of someone, you don't just dislike them — you look down on them. You see them as so low, so unworthy, so beneath you that they barely deserve your attention. It is disrespect mixed with superiority.
Understanding the Feeling Behind It

To truly understand "contemptuous," you need to understand the noun it comes from: contempt.

Contempt is not ordinary dislike. It is a cold, dismissive feeling — the sense that something or someone is so inferior that they are almost beneath the effort of being angry at. It's different from hatred, because hatred often implies that someone matters enough to stir strong emotion. Contempt says: "You are not even worth my real emotion. You are beneath me."

Think of it like a scale of disrespect:

  • Mild disrespect → you don't think much of someone
  • Dislike → you have a negative feeling toward them
  • Scorn → you mock or reject them sharply
  • Contempt → you view them as fundamentally worthless, inferior, or beneath your level

Contemptuous is the adjective form of that last and most powerful stage.
The Three Core Ingredients

For something to be truly contemptuous, it usually involves three things working together:

1. A sense of superiority — The contemptuous person believes they are above the other person (or thing). They are looking down, not across.

2. Total dismissal — The person or thing being treated with contempt is considered not worthy of real respect, engagement, or consideration.

3. An outward show — Contemptuous doesn't just mean feeling this way inside. The adjective specifically describes the expression or display of that feeling — through words, looks, tone, body language, or behavior.
Examples in Sentences

Here are clear examples to show you exactly how the word works:

  • "She gave him a contemptuous look when he suggested she couldn't do the job herself."
    Her look communicated: you are beneath me, and your doubt is not worth my respect.
  • "He spoke in a contemptuous tone about people who didn't read books."
    His tone showed he looked down on those people as inferior or ignorant.
  • "The general was contemptuous of the enemy's strategy, dismissing it as amateur and foolish."
    He viewed the enemy's thinking as so poor it didn't even deserve serious consideration.
  • "Her contemptuous laugh stung more than any insult would have."
    A laugh can be contemptuous when it signals: you are so ridiculous, you aren't even worth arguing with.
  • "He was openly contemptuous of the rules, treating them as things that only applied to lesser people."
    He saw the rules as beneath him — something unworthy of his compliance.
What It Looks Like in Real Life

Contemptuous behavior can show up in many forms. Here are the most common ones:

  • A sneer or smirk — a facial expression that signals mockery and superiority
  • A dismissive wave of the hand — as if to say "you are not worth engaging with"
  • Sarcastic or belittling speech — talking to someone as if they are a child or a fool
  • Ignoring or talking over someone — treating their words as unworthy of attention
  • Eye-rolling — a classic contemptuous gesture, signaling that what someone said is laughably beneath serious thought
  • A mocking, cold laugh — laughing at someone, not with them

When a person is described as contemptuous, you can almost picture them with raised eyebrows, a cold expression, and a slightly curled lip — looking at someone the way a person might look at something unpleasant on the bottom of their shoe.
How Strong Is This Word?

"Contemptuous" is a strong word. It is not used for mild or casual disrespect. You wouldn't call someone contemptuous just because they were a little rude or impolite. This word signals a deep, usually sustained attitude of looking down on someone or something. It carries emotional weight and suggests a clear hierarchy in the speaker's mind — I am above you.
Synonyms — and How They Differ

These words are close to "contemptuous," but each has a slightly different flavor:

  • Scornful — very similar to contemptuous, often used interchangeably. Scornful leans slightly more toward active mockery or rejection.
  • Disdainful — similar in meaning, but disdainful often feels a bit more cold and distant. A disdainful person might simply refuse to engage, whereas a contemptuous person might openly sneer.
  • Disparaging — focused specifically on belittling comments or speech. You can be disparaging without the full weight of superiority that "contemptuous" carries.
  • Condescending — talking or acting as if you are superior to someone. Condescending is similar but tends to be more about patronizing someone (treating them like a child), whereas contemptuous is more about dismissing them entirely.
  • Haughty — proud, arrogant, and acting superior — but haughty focuses more on the person's own self-image, while contemptuous focuses on how they treat others.
Antonyms — The Opposite

Understanding the opposites helps cement the meaning:

  • Respectful — showing consideration and regard for someone's worth
  • Admiring — looking up to someone, thinking highly of them
  • Reverential — showing deep respect, almost awe
  • Deferential — showing humble respect by yielding to another's judgment or status
A Critical Distinction: Contemptuous vs. Contemptible

This is one of the most common confusions with this word, so pay close attention:

  • Contemptuous = showing contempt. It describes the person (or their look, tone, behavior) who is doing the looking down.
    "He was contemptuous of her."* → He is the one looking down.
  • Contemptible = deserving contempt. It describes the person or thing being looked down upon as worthy of that scorn.
    "His behavior was contemptible."* → His behavior was so bad that it deserves to be looked down upon.

Easy memory trick: Contemptuous = full of contempt (like someone who is full of something). Contemptible = able to attract contempt (like something terrible enough to earn it).
Can "Contemptuous" Ever Be Positive?

No. Contemptuous is always a negative word. However, depending on the context, a contemptuous attitude might be understandable or even justified in the reader's eyes. For example, if a character is contemptuous of a corrupt, cruel tyrant, the reader might sympathize with that contempt — but the word itself still describes a harsh, dismissive attitude. The word is descriptive, not approving.
Quick Summary

Contemptuous means openly showing that you think someone or something is worthless, inferior, and beneath your respect. It combines a feeling of superiority with a visible expression of dismissal. It's a strong word — stronger than mere rudeness or dislike. When someone is contemptuous, they aren't just being unkind; they're signaling that they view the other person (or thing) as beneath them entirely.
